# OA v0.7.21

**Status:** Public development preview

**Release date:** 2026-08-28

**Source:** [`v0.7.21`](https://github.com/realminc/oa/releases/tag/v0.7.21)

## Summary

OA v0.7.21 publishes the private `v0.7.2` foundation performance and security
checkpoint together with the private `v0.7.3` container-naming closure. It
hardens the OA-owned foundation, adds explicit host-memory policies, restores
clear vendored Vulkan-loader and allocator boundaries, and removes the
ambiguous pre-1.0 `oa::Vec` container spelling.

The recorded speedups are scoped fixed-host measurements with correctness
oracles. They are not universal performance, security-certification, or
cross-platform claims.

## Highlights

- Foundation contracts now reject audited overflow, invalid synchronization
  state, stale aliasing, partial construction, moved-from container, embedded
  NUL, and incomplete secret-erasure failure modes.
- `oa::memcpy` keeps fixed-size compiler lowering and tuned bulk fallback;
  explicit `memcpyStream`, `memzeroSecure`, `memEqual`, and
  `memEqualConstantTime` expose cache and secret-handling policy.
- VKL and the AMD-derived VMA source live under the documented third-party
  boundary with exact provenance. OA runtime integration remains owned by
  `oa::Engine`.
- The engine upload-cache lookup changes from a linear scan to an ordered
  capacity index while retaining smallest-sufficient reuse.
- The generic owning sequence is now `oa::Vector<T>`; VLM keeps the distinct
  `oa::vlm::Vec2`, `Vec3`, and `Vec4` mathematical types.

## Compatibility and migration

- Replace `oa::Vec<T>` with `oa::Vector<T>`.
- Replace `<oa/core/std/vec.h>` with `<oa/core/std/vector.h>`.
- No compatibility alias or forwarding header is provided. Rebuild all native
  consumers and discard pre-1.0 binary caches.
- The VMA façade and VKL loader remain private implementation dependencies;
  public OA allocator ownership and Vulkan value contracts remain unchanged.

## Performance

On the recorded Clang 22.1.8, glibc 2.44, Intel Core i5-1145G7 host:

- `HashMap` and `HashSet` insertion used 34.1% and 35.1% of host-library time
  in the expanded foundation benchmark.
- Dynamic 8-byte and 32-byte copies used 49.8% and 66.3% of libc time; larger
  ordinary copies were near parity.
- Explicit cache-cold streaming copies used 79.2-83.9% of libc time for the
  accepted 64 KiB through 4 MiB ML-sized rows, except 256 KiB at 86.1%.
- VMA small-vector spill/refill used 68.7% of pristine AMD time. Two VMA cases
  remained at parity, while virtual allocate/free and a 32-byte clone remained
  7.2% and 8.8% slower because checked contracts were retained.
- The 4,096-entry engine upload-cache gate measured 117.067 ns/reuse after
  removing the linear scan, versus 60,295.077 ns/reuse at the historical
  baseline. Thermal spread and machine scope remain explicit in the VMA report.

Full methodology, absolute values, process ranges, rejected experiments, and
non-claims are recorded in the
[foundation benchmark](../benchmarks/oaStd.md). The VMA and allocator-policy
evidence is owned by the source documentation published with this checkpoint.

## Known limitations

- Linux x86-64 is the qualified runtime host for the new foundation and VMA
  measurements. Other OS, compiler, architecture, driver, and device matrices
  remain open.
- Binary independence, extended allocation-fault injection, long-running fuzz
  campaigns, and hostile-input qualification remain unfinished.
- `Vector` reserved scalar push retains a compiler-control-flow gap, mutex
  lock/unlock retains checked-wrapper overhead, and single-thread
  `SharedPtr` copy retains atomic ownership where the measured host library
  uses process-state non-atomic behavior.
- Vulkan Video and GPU paths remain capability-, queue-, driver-, and
  device-dependent; unsupported routes fail closed.

## Upgrade

Rebuild C++ and Python consumers, apply the `oa::Vector` source migration,
regenerate owned sources, and discard stale build, package, execution-plan,
model, checkpoint, and pre-1.0 binary caches. Validate workload-specific
performance on the deployment hardware rather than transferring the recorded
laptop ratios as universal expectations.
